title: Rav Ashi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Of this towering genius, who built for us the house of Israel — an everlasting building, a mighty and strong building, a building into which he breathed the breath of life, a speaking spirit for the whole nation, and called it by the name “Babylonian Talmud” — nothing is known to us of his ancestry: nowhere are his forebears or family named. The scholar Graetz, in part 2, p. 431, says: “Rabbana Ashi bar Shimi, a scion of a stock of venerable Torah scholars; while still young he had made a name for himself as a man of exalted standing above all the Torah scholars of his generation and his land, and he was taken with honor to be head of the academy in Sura, which is Mata Mechasya … When he was chosen as head of the academy he was still young — if not fourteen years old, as some chroniclers of the generations hold, in any case not more than twenty … and of the days of his youth, the course of his education and the ways of his learning nothing is known to us.”
End of quotation. This scholar does not mention, even in passing, who his teachers were — as though an angel had come and taught him the whole Torah on one foot.
The rabbi and scholar Isaac Hirsch Weiss followed him in Dor Dor veDorshav, part 3, chapter 17. Hyman quotes him as follows:

“Rav Ashi was of a family of sages; his father was Rav Shimi bar Ashi, a distinguished man, etc. Rav Ashi was born on the day Rava died. His distinguished teacher was Rav Kahana the third (who headed the academy in Pumbedita and died in 725 (תשכה) — 4173 (ד״א קעג) — thirteen years before Rav Ashi) … Indeed, his stay before his teachers did not last long, for while still very young he was chosen to be head of the academy in Sura; and although we cannot believe what the legend told, that he was fourteen when he became academy head, it is nonetheless clear that at the beginning of his headship he was young … And their practice (in Rav Ashi’s academy) was to arrange two tractates every year, and the arrangement of the whole Talmud lasted thirty years. In this too the Lord helped him and his desire prospered in his hand, for He gave him length of days and kept him alive in the land nearly eighty years, and he stood to review his arrangement once again and made of the Talmud two editions.” End of quotation. Hyman understands his view to be that Rav Ashi became academy head when about twenty and held that position nearly sixty years, and that his days of life were nearly eighty years; and so the scholar Graetz wrote in part 2, p. 433.

Hyman rejects all their words as errors from beginning to end, advancing these objections: that Rav Shimi bar Ashi was not his father; that he was not fourteen when he became academy head — and in which legend did they find this falsehood? — and not twenty either, but he was already advanced in years; that Rav Kahana who headed the academy in Pumbedita was not his teacher; that he was not born when Rava died, but rather merited to be Rava’s student; that he was almost unique in several generations in having received teachings from all the great men of his generation, and his teachers were many; and that his days of life were much more than eighty years.

notes.text: This supplied notice is an introductory polemic, not a complete Rav Ashi biography. The Graetz and R.A.H.W. quotations are translated from Hyman’s Hebrew renderings, not newly checked against those authors. The supplied work abbreviation is דו״ד; the old draft’s categorical Dorot HaRishonim expansion is withdrawn as unsupported. The author/work identification remains a bibliographic question. תשכה and ד״א קעג are rendered725 and4173 as given, without asserting their era conversion or equivalence. Hyman’s replies about parentage, teachers, age at appointment and lifespan retain their categorical force as his arguments. In the supplied final list האחר literally suggests the last/other, while the context may suggest האחד (the one/unique); neither alternative is silently substituted. That wording remains held. Academy leadership, not kingship, is intended by מלך.

The unresolved work abbreviation and האחר reading are separate questions. Neither is settled by the preceding authors’ competing age calculations; those calculations and Hyman’s objections are preserved as attributed arguments.

The cited modern sources have not been directly collated here: Graetz, part 2, pp. 431 and 433, and the work supplied as דו״ד, part 3, chapter 17. Catalogue routing lists Dor Dor veDorshav, part 3, by Isaac Hirsch Weiss, and a secondary quotation resembles the passage; neither establishes the exact cited edition, wording or abbreviation by direct comparison. The attempted book/catalogue retrievals did not provide the chapter text. The Hebrew renderings, dates, competing ages and Hyman’s categorical objections therefore remain attributed to Hyman and the writers he quotes. No parentage, teacher, chronology, lifespan or emended reading of האחר is admitted.

The earlier notes record the questions before the printed witnesses were checked. The initials ראה״ו and the title abbreviated דו״ד refer to Isaac Hirsch Weiss’s Dor Dor veDorshav, vol. III, ch. 17. The consulted scan, pp. 183–184 and 187, contains the matching account of Rav Ashi’s family, principal teacher, early appointment, and work on the Talmud. Weiss and Hyman’s printed quotation include a tenure of nearly sixty years within the quotation itself. The supplied text omits that clause and gives the nearly sixty years afterward in Hyman’s summary. The translation keeps that arrangement.

Hyman’s printed vol. I, p. 244, reads האחד (“the one”), whereas the supplied transcription reads האחר (“the other” or “the last”). The English “almost unique” follows the printed clause in Hyman’s list of objections. The same page prints שאר רוח in the Graetz quotation, in place of supplied שאר אוח. The cited pages of Graetz, part 2, pp. 431 and 433, remain uncollated.

Kiddushin 72b places Rav Ashi’s birth when Rava died. Rambam’s introduction to the Mishneh Torah lists Rav Ashi and Ravina among those who received the tradition from Rava. Niddah 51a records objections by Rav Ashi in the discussion of Rava’s position, and Rashi explicitly directs one to Rava. These are the transmission and textual witnesses relevant to Hyman’s disagreement. Bava Batra 157b distinguishes earlier and later teaching of a particular ruling. Weiss’s account of two recensions of the Talmud is his interpretation of such evidence.
